speechtext:
It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair until 8 p.m.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. At six o'clock the Minister of State (Small Businesses) had the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner hour I made a few comments which I hope will correct some misunderstandings and misapprehensions which exist. I can see some hon. members opposite are still in doubt; some of them take a little longer to understand the facts than others. I attempted on authoritative grounds to show that ten years of Liberal government since 1968, far from being the kind of dismal years that have been reflected upon by the opposition, have indeed been years of great growth, great prosperity and great creation of job opportunities.
Unlike the Tory opposition desperately craving power at the risk of distorting the facts, I have been citing factual evidence to support my proposition. I suggest it is an ill-service to the country for the opposition to take the kind of tack they have been taking. I also said, and again I suggest authoritatively, on the basis of any knowledgeable, fair-minded observer, including those in the small business community that have reason to know, such as Mr. John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, that there is no country in the world today which has better tax incentives for small business than Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the United States?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I include in that the United States.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. Minister of State has the floor and I suggest we all listen.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Your judgments are always good but I strongly recommend that one.
In order to supplement this statement of fact I would like to spend a few moments relating some of these tax incentives, not simply those of the recent budget but those of the more recent past.
Of course, the most important of these is the low rate of corporate tax and the dividend gross-up and credit. As hon. members are aware, the small incorporated businessman with income below $ 150,000 per year or retained earnings of up to $750,000 pays some 20 to 21 percentage points below that of the larger business.
In addition, under the new system of the dividend gross-up and credit an individual who is the recipient of earnings from

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
an incorporated small business, under the small business tax rate, enjoys a substantially lower marginal income tax rate than that of wage earner, salary earner or person earning dividends from a larger business. For instance, a taxpayer with $30,000 of income pays only 26 per cent on additional income received from a small incorporated business. A wage or salary or unincorporated business income would bear a 46 per cent marginal tax rate. The high income taxpayers also enjoy a significant tax deferral on their income from incorporated small businesses. As long as the income is retained in a corporation it bears the low corporation rate of 25 per cent. It is only upon the eventual distribution that the taxpayer pays; then in the case of the high income earner it would be substantially above those at the corporate level. So that there is a distinct saving for those choosing to invest in small businesses in this form.
In addition, in the 1977 budget there was permitted employee stock option liberalization. This provides that employees of a small business can receive options, and it is only when they sell their stock that they pay tax and then it is at the capital gains rate rather than at the higher rate of tax they would pay if it was in the form of earnings.
Family farms, both incorporated and unincorporated, may now be transferred to other members of the family free from tax, whereas in the past this has not been the case. Again, this is a measure most beneficial to those who have an interest in family farms and I believe hon. members opposite who take an interest in agriculture are gratified by this measure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We shall take the credit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Take the credit if you will but at least acknowledge the benefit.
Another great benefit which is available under this beneficent regime which has been so widely criticized is in the area of income splitting among family members in corporations. Family members can now be employed in an incorporated business and receive incomes. Anyone familiar with this situation will know that members of a family who own or share in an enterprise can now receive income from it at substantially lower tax rates than they would pay if they were receiving it as one income from the business, as is the case with an unincorporated business.
There are a number of other benefits, such as the elimination of federal sales taxes for small producers of handicrafts; the deferral of capital gains on voluntary sales of fixed assets, thereby allowing firms to relocate without the penalty of taxation; the option offered to venture capital investors to choose whether to be taxed on a capital gains basis or on the basis of ordinary income. An amendment to Part IV dealing with refundable tax removes the hindrance imposed on corporate investors taking a minority interest in other businesses. There is assistance with respect to metric conversion by tradesmen and retailers. There is a 3 per cent inventory allowance, and a provision for making expenditures on research and

development admissible for tax credit. An increase in the dividend tax credit has been made and in the field of capital gains the present $1,000 exemption has been extended.
I have not covered all the ground, Mr. Speaker, but I have listed examples which go a long way to back up the proposition I have advanced, namely that far from having suffered from a system which is inferior to that in other countries the small businessman in Canada, as is acknowledged by small businessmen and experts in this field, enjoys tax benefits superior to those in any other country in the world.
In my opinion, the Minister of Finance has added to these various incentives by the most direct and positive measure which could be carried out in the circumstances facing him by applying a direct reduction in the sales tax of 3 per cent. The obvious benefit of this is that it places purchasing power directly in the hands of the consumer, thereby creating an incentive for the consumer to spend money at the local retail level. So far from describing the tax system of this country as detrimental to small business, far from regarding the budget as having done no thing for small business, the combination of this budget and th ; budget of March, 1977, together with the tax apparatus which has been set up in the past, goes a long way to adding to incentives for small business people to set up business.
Nobody, least of all myself, suggests there is not or will not be room in the future for further improvements. I think all of us could, in inventive moments, think of areas in which improvements in the tax system could take place. Perhaps modifications in the capital gains tax division, the possible creation of small business investment companies which could take advantage of the tax system and draw capital for investment in small business are good examples. There is the Bank Act which the hon. member opposite speaks of.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When it comes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, when it is brought in I am sure hon. members will find that it, too, contains measures which will be beneficial to the country and beneficial to the small business community and to new entries in the banking field.
We who are working very hard in this area of small business need not stop, however, at describing the benefits under the tax system, happy and progressive though it is. There have been a number of other improvements which have done a great deal to give heart to the small business community. One of the most important concerns the Small Businesses Loans Act.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) says "Oh!" I can assure him that when I was up in his constituency the other day businessmen in Bracebridge were delighted to hear about the improvement in that act.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Flear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The legislation was amended in the spring to raise the limit to $75,000. Recently the interest rate was
April 18, 1978

amended. Small businessmen are now encouraged to find they will be able to borrow money under the act to expand their businesses, and these amendments will really do a great deal. I have spoken to representatives of the chartered banks and they have assured me that this act has hitherto not been an inducement. Yet last year, despite the fact they claimed they lost money, they lent as much as $80 million. So I believe that with the improvements in the legislation we shall now see a real volume of business being done to help the small business community.
I turn to the activities of the Federal Business Development Bank. Here is an institution which has served the Canadian businessman well. It now has nearly $2 billion in loans outstanding, having lent over $300 million last year. Its affairs are being conducted by an aggressive new management with new ideas, and I believe that this bank, too, will prove of even greater assistance to the small business community than it has in the past.
We also have the CASE program under the direction of the Federal Business Development Bank. Here is an important program which is being offered to the small business community. Almost 2,000 consultants drawn mainly from retired business people are advising at low or nominal fees and showing small businessmen how to improve their management techniques. Dun and Bradstreet, a firm specializing in bankruptcies, indicates that 90 per cent of bankruptcies are caused by poor management. Failure among small businessmen is all too frequently brought about by a lack of understanding of management techniques. The Government of Canada, through the CASE program, is bringing assistance to them which is unavailable in any other form at the price.
In addition, we have taken an important new initiative in moving toward the reduction of the paper burden by the creation of an office in government whose purpose is to reduce the paper burden on small business.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hurrah for that!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that expression of enthusiastic support. I suggest that progress will be made, that we shall shortly see some demonstrable results from this program and that there will be far fewer forms to be filled in by business people and a great deal less government interference with their daily work.
I am sorry there is so little time available to me in which to give a fuller resume of all the things this government has tried to do for the small businessman. Recently we opened a small business centre in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce staffed by a knowledgeable group of people who are there when visiting businessmen come to Ottawa. They will not only tell them where to go; they will help them with their problems, assist them in making appointments and give them advice with regard to government programs.
In addition, this small business centre has a "hot line" which anybody in Canada can call. The number is Zenith 03200.
The Budget-Mr. Abbott
Anybody can call and get an answer which does not pass the buck but which really gives a response. I urge the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka to call that number when he gets home, to see if I am right.
While many other governments would sit back and ask who could do more, this government is not prepared to rest on its laurels, deserving as it may be. It is not prepared simply to acknowledge that in the last ten years Canada has enjoyed a growth and prosperity unequalled by any other country in the world with the exception of Japan.
We are now looking at a number of positive incentives such as the one I mentioned, the creation of small business investment companies and the setting up of venture development centres to help small businessmen who want to get into business find people with money.
The other day I sent a couple of officials up to Whitehorse, where they spent three days because we are very concerned that not just the great corporations which are making steel pipe or making valves, etc., receive the benefits of the pipeline. We are interested in seeing that the small business community also enjoys the benefits. When those officials returned they advised me that there is a great deal of enthusiasm in that community, and I believe we can do much to help them.
In addition to these positive, beneficial and progressive ideas and programs, responsible programs were enunciated in the budget by the Minister of Finance who, notwithstanding difficult times, accepted his responsibility, delivered a sober, constructive and responsible budget, and yet offered Canadians incentives.
What are we getting from the desperate crowd of power-hungry politicians opposite, who crave above all else to sit on this side of the House, probably by their desperation and irresponsibility permanently denying themselves that privilege forever?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What we get from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) are reckless suggestions that they would cut taxes by up to $3 billion. They would restrain government spending and do a lot of other things at the same time.
Mr. White way: You are right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member says I am right. He is the only one who believes it because the Canadian people are not going to buy that kind of rubbish. The Canadian people will listen to that kind of irresponsibility and ask themselves whether they are satisfied to hear "Joe Who?"-the Leader of the Opposition-enunciate what he is going to do for the economy when he cannot even secure a seat in his own home town. Canadians will ask themselves whether they should listen to a man who is trying to urge upon his colleagues that same sense of irresponsibility. His colleagues are a feeble army of financial critics who are, to serve their own ends, attempting to foster in the minds of the Canadian people an apprehension that this country is going down the drain.
4634

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Mr. F. Hamilton
No, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the people of this country will consider the responsible statements of the Minister of Finance. They will see where this country stands after ten years of Liberal government, and I suggest they will reject the gloom and doom we hear from the opposition and once again demonstrate at the polls just where they think the Tory party should reside.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the minister's assurance that our banking system will now use the new Small Businesses Loans Act, because in the past it and the Farm Credit Act have been major stumbling blocks. Our banking system has been hesitant to use those two acts.
If I understood the minister correctly, he said that last year some $80 million was lent under the Small Businesses Loans Act. At the maximum rate of $75,000 per businessman, that amounts only to just over 1,000 loans, so I think that is not a record to be proud of.
It seems obvious that this parliament is winding down. The sooner we go to the country, the better, because this government has almost overwhelmed Canada with its permissiveness, disunity and economic incompetence in the past decade. The budget indicates no basic change in the philosophy of this government. Generally speaking, if you tax something, you get less of it; if you subsidize something, you tend to get more of it. The approach of this government is still the same. It continues to tax work, growth, investment, employment, savings and productivity and to subsidize no work, consumption and debt. Ten years is enough!
Ten years ago we were a nation proud of our heritage, confident in our capabilities and purpose and sure of our direction and destiny in world affairs. It was this confidence and purpose which held together our widely scattered provinces and racial groups. Today, however, this spirit of national unity and purpose has given way to doubts, fears and uncertainties in every province.
Even ten short years ago there were few Canadians who were not convinced that Canada had the capacity, resources and will to survive as a strong and independent North American nation. Any suggestions of separation or of joining with the United States would have been ridiculed. Indeed, we assumed that the rest of the world envied the strength of our judicial structure, the soundness of our banking system and economic policies and the integrity and reputation of our police forces. Our stability, respect for law and order and educational standards were all matters of great pride.
However, in the span of only a few years much of this solid structure has crumbled, and we now find ourselves groping and wondering just what has happened so suddenly. Canadians are weary of inflation, bureaucracy, political scandals and the false promises of our leaders. They are tired of the shopworn government we have which no longer commands respect. People generally are sick of the new morality which seems to have something in it to offend everyone.

What are the answers, and is a cure possible? If we continue this downhill slide while at the same time having resources of all kinds, we are certainly headed for an ultimate bust if we do not learn a few simple lessons. The picture may be bleak, but it is not hopeless.
Canada is one of the wealthiest nations on earth, yet we look with envy on the Arabs. We over-react to the significance of their energy wealth. Certainly they have oil, and lots of it, but they are lacking in many resources, particularly the human resources which we have in Canada.
In Canada we, too, have oil and natural gas. We also have tremendous forests, agricultural reserves, coal, iron ore, nickel, lead, uranium; you name it. And probably the greatest wealth of all, not often thought about, is our water. Imagine what the Middle East would give for an ample supply of fresh water. The Arabian countries have lots of oil, but they are short of welders, electricians, carpenters, engineers, chemists and pipe fitters. We have them in abundance, and it is this great Canadian resource of skilled people that we have to take advantage of.
The Japanese have virtually no resources. All they really have going for them are about 90 million workers who have some incentive to work. Imagine what our agricultural producers and small business people could do if they could just have a tax-free kitty to put a few dollars into in good years, to be drawn upon in poor years.
We have to upgrade the resources which leave this country. The natural gas which goes south to the United States comes back in the form of plastic. Wood from our forests goes south and across the Pacific and comes back as furniture or plywood. Our coal and iron ore which go to Japan come back as Toyotas. Probably half of the goods purchased by our overtaxed workers is made elsewhere, from coal, oil, natural gas, wood or other materials, extracted from this country.
In order to upgrade our raw materials we must have a climate to encourage investment in Canadian manufacturing. Since the end of the World War II we have visibly lost strength and status among the world's more powerful industrial nations. We have tended to concentrate on redistributing the wealth we have rather than creating new wealth.
We may well look at Germany's economic miracle after World War II. They proceeded on the basis that it was easier to give everyone a larger slice out of a bigger cake than to gain anything by fighting over the division of a smaller cake. The German government did three things: the first was to abolish state planning and end price controls; second, they established freedom for the consumer to buy what he likes and recognize his freedom to work with or without union membership as a basic right of every citizen; third, they encouraged greater productivity of goods to help bring down prices. They established a 48-hour work week and overtime wages were made tax free.
We cannot find a solution in Canada by still more spending and more borrowing for social services and less individual
April 18, 1978

incentive. We cannot serve long term unemployment through more welfare because it will only bring another generation into being as wards of the Crown. Our problems will not be solved outside this country. The job is internal and the unity of our country will never be secured with a sick economy.
So is it any wonder that our people are bitter when we see American TV ads for automobiles which are $2,000 cheaper than our automobiles? It is particularly irritating when a good number of people realize that the automobile in question was manufactured in Canada. Home appliances are offered at substantially lower prices in the United States. Many U.S. models are identical to Canadian models built in Canada by the same company with headquarters in the U.S. Housing prices are much higher in Canada. Also, mortgage interest rates at time are more than double here, and they are not tax deductible as they are in the U.S. Higher and higher personal income taxes required to pay for social programs all add to this frustration.
One of our real problems in Canada has been the failure of our federal government to bargain properly with the public sector. Salary scales have gone completely out of control, putting undue pressure on the private sector to equal the wage gains of government employees.
However, I believe the attitude in Canada is changing and that we are going to recognize that a restoration of the incentive system is really the only way to bring about prosperity. We should be using our energy surplus and our great natural resources to negotiate bilateral trade agreements with the United States in particular, with Japan and the European Economic Community, to promote substantial growth in the manufacturing sector in this country.
It does not seem unreasonable, if we agree to export several hundred million cubic feet of natural gas to the United States to assist in their gas shortage situation, if we ask that some of the export be in the form of manufactured products derived from Canadian natural gas. Indications are the United States is willing to discuss such an agreement. The United States being our principal trading partner, this is the logical place to start.
One of the fictions we have been living under for the past decade, and it is a most insidious one, is that our political rights guarantee equality in all things. This has come to mean equality not only at the starting line but at the finish line as well. Well, I just do not believe it. We should all have equality, not only at the starting line, but while the race is on. The guarantee should be freedom-freedom to achieve or to fail, freedom to make the most of every talent and ability we have, and freedom to run the race as best we can. Finally, we should have freedom to receive the rewards of that effort. We need a change in policy, attitudes and outlook, a new Canada with a new government.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak out and express my opinion on the budget, especially in these hard times. Mr. Speaker, this
The Budget-Mr. Allard
budget must be considered in light of the present economic and political situation. No budget can be made in a vacuum, without regard for the reality of the day. I would like to consider some blatant examples of the way the government persists in giving everything to the rich and nothing to the poor.
But first I would like to comment on the 2 per cent provincial sales tax rebate that the government has proposed. Once again it is the low income earner who will foot the bill because the government will have to take this money somewhere or else transfer it to the already heavy debt. Furthermore, the government should have offered solutions that come under its jurisdiction and not act on behalf of the provinces. I am not against federal aid in a sense, but that should only occur after certain other measures are taken such as lowering the federal tax, increasing the basic exemption from $2,700 to at least $4,000, the government should also have increased the excise tax on products we could easily produce ourselves here in Canada. With regard to the controversy that opposes the Quebec government to that in Ottawa, to my mind, having a protectionist policy is not turning everything upside down. I feel the proposal of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was not adapted to the needs in Quebec. Hardly any automobiles are manufactured there and a 2 per cent reduction on that product would not have helped the province. The last budget proves that this government is unable to apply measures that take into consideration the particular needs of the provinces generally.
I should now like to discuss the amounts earmarked for research and development. The new tax credits the government proposes for R & D are another example of inadequate solutions to current problems. The government wants to allow companies to deduct 50 per cent of their additional expenditures on R & D. Applied research especially is involved here, as new technologies are wanted to improve existing products. However, those new tax credits favour big business which already enjoys the benefit of other government measures. But nothing is being done to help independent researchers. The situation of the researcher in Canada is unacceptable. Allow me to quote a paragraph from the article by Margaret Munro, published in the Ottawa Citizen on April 10, 1978, on the lack of efficient government assistance to research, and I quote:

This sort of unexpected oscillation is not only destroying Canada's medical research community but it's costing the taxpayer millions of dollars. A researcher spends six months setting up his lab and the next thing you know he loses his grant, he says.

It is truly unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, that a researcher should have to live in financial and material poverty in Canada. It is also unbelievable that in his budget the Minister of Finance did not provide concrete measures to help research and development in hospitals and universities.
80038-4Vi

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Allard
I would like to quote some questions submitted by Dr. John Kucharczyk, executive secretary of scientific policies of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies, to my colleague the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):

Is the Canadian neglect of scientific research more serious in some sectors, i.e. universities, than in others? Is the neglect concentrated in particular areas, i.e. social sciences and natural sciences?

Mr. Speaker, we of the Social Credit Party of Canada say that the measures put forward in the budgets last year and this year do not meet the real needs of Canadians. These measures tend to favour research and development through tax deductions. This is effective for the government in office because it attracts favours and election funds from large companies. This explains the cuts which were made to the funds allocated to medical research at the university level. Given the shortsightedness of Liberal members, the government hastens to tell the people that funds earmarked for pure research done mainly in universities should be cut to increase the funds allocated to applied or industrial research.
Another question read as follows, and I quote:
Your party is on record as favouring an increase in R & D investment in the public and private sector from the current level of less than 1 per cent of the gross national product to 2.5 per cent of the GNP. What effect do you believe that an increase in Canadian R & D would have on the nation's economy?

We reply that the most obvious effect of research is the greater technological and consequently economic independence from neighbouring countries, especially the United States. Research is the only way to make our industries more competitive on the international market. Moreover, this will promote the hiring of more employees in research laboratories. From a medical point of view, it is a known fact that research improves the health of the population who can then have more productive activities.
Finally, only research and its effects can bring a final solution to the great problems of our times, such as unemployment, inflation, control over Canada's 200 mile zone and the protection of our environment. If the minister has understood what we have just said, he will agree that research and development can bring solutions to our economic problems, whether in the area of agriculture, of pulp and paper or elsewhere.
I would now like to say a few words about our debt. Another one of the false solutions proposed by the minister in his budget is the debt. We must wonder if the minister is aware of the definiton of debt. The Larousse dictionary gives one and it is not necessary to be Minister of Finance to understand it. At page 313 of the Larousse dictionary, we find the following definition: Something owed, an obligation. Mr. Speaker, we

have an obligation of more than $11 billion. The debt for each Canadian worker amounts to $10,600. Every newborn in Canada owes this amount from the date of his birth.
Last Thursday, during question period, there was reference to the sales tax quarrel between Quebec and Ottawa. My colleague from Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) asked the Minister of Finance if he could use the Bank of Canada to create new credits to increase the money supply. The minister replied that he had looked into the social credit theories as early as 1963 and that he was convinced that he was right to oppose them. But, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance is really serious, he should start to learn social credit philosophy and he would find out that if foreign investors consider Canadian bonds as valuable guarantees for their loans to the Government of Canada, our own bank, the Bank of Canada, could accept the same guarantees from the same government.
When foreign investors lend money to this country, they know that the wealth and labour of Canadians are good guarantees to buy Canadian bonds. So why should those who have been elected by Canadians not take their own responsibilities? And instead of maintaining a debt system, let us have a credit system so that Canadians may get rid of this debt system and perform as a sovereign people. Those same guarantees accepted by foreigners should also be accepted by the Bank of Canada and thus it would be able to monetize the credit of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, how can the minister understand our philosophy when he does not even know what a debt is? Since the minister does not understand the basis of the economy, how can he put forward a sound budget? Current issues which can destroy Canada are not explained by the nature of this country but by the way it is governed. So, Mr. Speaker, there is only one solution and that is to elect a Social Credit government at next election.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the budget debate there are always a number of matters a person would like to refer to, given the latitude one is able to exercise in debate, but tonight I want to deal with the major fiscal proposal which appeared in the budget, in fact the only fiscal proposal of any significance, and this is the proposed reduction in provincial sales tax.
But to do that, Mr. Speaker, we must enter the world of Alice in Wonderland, where words mean what the federal government chooses them to mean; where a hasty round of telephone calls becomes full consultation; where a proposal which was mentioned briefly in October, revived suddenly at the end of March, and then firmed up after six provincial budgets came down, is said to have undergone extensive negotiation; a world where Claude Ryan becomes a separatist and Allan Blakeney a closet Tory. That is the Alice in Wonderland world which characterizes the government's tax cut proposal.
April 18, 1978

Nevertheless, let us proceed. We begin with a proposal clearly and solely in the field of provincial jurisdiction, one obviously requiring full partnership between the federal and provincial governments to ensure its success. Not only was the opportunity to forge such a partnership in budget making missed, but it was missed because no serious effort was made by the federal government to achieve it. Yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said the following:
... for the first time in Canadian history we have achieved a certain level of co-ordination of fiscal policy between the federal and the provincial governments.
As we look back at this past week, all we can say is: some level, some achievement. Meanwhile in his remarks on the budget, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) referred to the tremendous progress made by the government in the area of federal-provincial co-operation. He stated that after the tax cut period there may be the following:
... other new, imaginative and creative ideas flowing from this unique process which was introduced by the Prime Minister, and reinforced in these last few days by the Minister of Finance.
Let us take a closer look at this "unique process" which the minister extols. I will tell hon. members what is unique about the government's process of federal-provincial relations. At a time when most other forces in the country are aiming for consolidation, co-operation and compromise in the interests of unity, the federal government stands uniquely alone in its tactics of divide and conquer. If the government is doing anything imaginatively and creatively, it is fostering division rather than unity, resentment rather than accommodation. The manner in which the sales tax cut was put into place is just the latest in a long list of divisive federal government actions.
What is almost amusing about the sales tax issue is the fact that, while government members applaud what they perceive as a step forward in federal-provincial relations, or as an outstanding example of federal-provincial fiscal co-ordination, they seem to be the only ones applauding. Certainly the four western premiers have stated that the budget move contradicted the spirit of federal-provincial co-operation and consultation, and they said it could be prejudicial to ongoing discussions on national unity.
The reaction of the province of Quebec to this step forward in federal-provincial relations has been anything but ecstatic. All political parties in that province, the new leader of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, and Quebec newspapers both English and French, have been unanimous in their criticism of the federal government's handling of the sales tax cut.
We have five of the ten provinces dissatisfied with the federal government's latest effort at federai-provincial co-operation. When one considers that, of the remaining five provinces, four do not have to make any financial contribution to the plan and the fifth was the originator of the idea, one can readily conclude that there is little reason to applaud the government's federal-provincial diplomacy.
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
It has long been my contention that the process of conducting federal-provincial relations requires as much sensitivity and consideration as do the substantive measures involved. Here, sir, in the government's sales tax proposal we have a concrete example of where their lack of sensitivity toward the process of federal-provincial relations has diminished the potential good in the substantive issue.
We on this side of the House have no quarrel with the sales tax cut in itself. We have said it is a good idea, and we have said that here in the House. We have, rather, argued that it will not be in effect long enough and that it will come to an end just when the winter unemployment season is beginning. It is not the measure in itself but how the measure was taken that invites the criticism, not just of the opposition, but of the House and of the provincial premiers, the very ones whose goodwill is essential to maintaining the plan or putting it into effect.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made much of the proposed success of the recent first ministers' economic summit conference which he billed as the beginning of a new era in federal-provincial relations. He and his ministers have exaggerated beyond belief the degree of agreement that was reached by all the premiers on this detail or on that detail. They were supposed to have discussed all the urgent matters of joint concern at that conference. It was the logical place to do so.
But now what do we find? We find that in the two months following that conference the federal government brings in two major initiatives, the referendum bill and the sales tax proposal, both of which are of great concern to the provinces and neither of which we find was discussed or even mentioned at that much-vaunted economic summit conference. The renewed sense of partnership that the Prime Minister sought and thought he had in the first ministers' conference does not exist. It was all a facade and sham, an exercise in public relations designed to brush up on appearances, but to accomplish little of substance. How else can we explain the failure of consultation in regard to both the referendum bill and the budget proposal?
The main point of discussion here today is the sales tax cut. But, sir, it is not the only recent deviation from that conference high in February. Another breakdown in federal-provincial relations is that complete lack of consultation with the provinces on the referendum legislation. A process to which so much importance should be attached is abandoned by the federal government whenever it is convenient for them to do so.
The minister in charge of federal-provincial relations, when questioned in the House about consultation with the premiers, stated that the referendum legislation covered only issues under federal jurisdiction, knowing full well, of course, that the referendum legislation addresses itself to any question relating to the constitution of Canada. He did admit at a press conference that it could be used in the case of failure to reach agreement with a province on constitutional matters, yet he

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
has either the naivety or audacity to suggest that all constitutional questions automatically fall within federal jurisdiction.
When the federal government is defining matters that fall within federal jurisdiction and providing the questions to be posed, how long would it be, given the record of this government, before the people of Canada were faced with national referenda on matters of joint jurisdiction such as authority over agricultural marketing boards, and then move on to subjects of disputed jurisdiction such as resources taxation, or even to subjects of strictly provincial jurisdiction such as post-secondary education?
We all need to be wary of the government's perspective of matters that fall within federal jurisdiction, but given their preoccupation with their own importance the federal government continues to be blind to the needs, the aspirations and to the wishes of the provinces, the other partners of confederation. More than that, the federal government is oblivious to their own blindness in this respect. When criticized about the failure to consult with the provinces on the budget proposals, the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance state: Oh, but we did consult with the provinces.
We all remember that phrase "profitable federalism". The federal government has their own version of that phrase. They were eager, indeed they were anxious, to have the provincial premiers at their side to endorse the generalities of their medium or midterm economic proposals. But when they had specific initiatives in mind, initiatives which would directly and immediately impact on the provinces, those proposals conveniently fell outside the boundaries of what could profitably be discussed at the first ministers' conference, even though the timing of the economic summit had been carefully chosen to give the first ministers the information they needed to adjust their budget planning in the light of the new proposals jointly agreed to at the time. The much vaunted mood of partnership that the Prime Minister spoke of, it now becomes clear, was taken seriously by the federal government only in so far as it served their own interests.
As I recall, looking back to that economic summit conference the general consensus at the close of the conference was that the federal government was the only government not to put forward a proposal. Now we know the reason why. It was not that they did not have proposals to make; it was just that they did not want to subject them to that forum. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance argue that the sales tax proposal had extensive discussion and that there was intensive co-operation over a period of six months. But when pushed, they reluctantly admit that it was raised briefly some six months ago and not by the federal government. Then it was allowed to lapse and only proceeded with a few weeks prior to the bringing down of the federal budget, after a flurry of telephone calls between the Minister of Finance and the provincial ministers on a one-to-one basis. At no time were the provinces able to discuss the matter among themselves, as would have been the case had the matter been properly brought up at the first ministers' conference in February. This is the place where it ought to have been discussed.

This kind of dealing is not consultation, and, further, bringing in a proposal which seriously affects provincial budgets after six provincial budgets have already been brought down is not co-operation. It was in some respects more akin to a lottery in which those provinces which bring down their budgets in April have a clear advantage over those which do so in March. The fact that four provinces were able to take the sales tax cuts into consideration in the budgets, with two provinces actually changing the dates and forms of their budgets-as the Prime Minister admitted yesterday-while six were not able to do so, give them a kind of special status and breeds resentment among the provinces. In no way does this exercise in federal bungling add up to partnership.
If you add to this, Mr. Speaker, the heavy-handed manner in which the government rejected the counter-proposal of Quebec, then the bungling becomes a fiasco. The handling of the sales tax with regard to the province of Quebec has been a disgrace, and when opposition members criticized the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance for their inept handling of this matter, what was the government's response? They lashed out and called all their critics separatists. That is their stock response to criticism of any stance regarding Quebec. To disagree with the Prime Minister is to want to break up the country.
So desperate was the Prime Minister in assailing his critics that he was able to perceive what had escaped everyone else- that Allan Blakeney was a closet supporter of the federal Progressive Conservative party. That was the claim he made. All of this might fit very well with the Prime Minister's image of himself as the saviour of the country, but it does not fit at all well with reality.
The Minister of Finance was proud of his sales tax proposal and the way in which it took into consideration certain regional realities. It has been flexible enough to give special consideration to the Atlantic provinces with full compensation and to allow two other provinces to opt for a smaller cut over a longer time. Yet when it comes to the province of Quebec, which has an even higher unemployment rate than two Atlantic provinces, the government took on the attitude of inflexiblity. All three political parties in the national assembly in the province of Quebec, the newly elected leader of the Liberal party in that province, and both the English and the French press, all came out in support of Quebec's position; but the federal government remained rigid in its stand.
In a move of apparent accommodation, the federal government then turned around and offered Quebec a supposedly new deal, which was in reality a new twist to its rigid position. Meanwhile, the federal money sits there as a reminder to the province of Quebec that there is only one set of rules by which to play the federal-provincial game, and those rules are set in Ottawa. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that faced with such domineering rigidity, the province of Quebec hurls accusations of paternalism and federal domination? Is it any wonder that in the space of ten years of such domineering rigidity, this country has a national unity problem that is fostered right here
April 18, 1978

in Ottawa? Does the Minister of Finance not realize that by his actions he lends credibility to the Parti Quebecois with allegations that Ottawa is paternalistic and domineering, or did he deliberately pick this fight? Did the minister deliberately pick this fight to shore up his government's sagging support in the rest of the country?
If this was his intent, his cynical manoeuvre served the tragic purpose of renewing fading support for a separatist government in the province of Quebec which he purports to oppose. The lesson to be learned here is that even a good idea badly executed works against itself.
It was with amazement yesterday that I listened to the Prime Minister express his puzzlement at the reaction of the western premiers. He said that they were upset, not about the content of the federal proposal, but about the form of its negotiation. That is precisely the point: given the blindness that I have already referred to on the part of this government, the Prime Minister will go on being puzzled as to why the western premiers are upset. The government has consistently overlooked the importance of the process through which negotiations are carried on, and in so doing has often jeopardized the substance of those proposals.
In federai-provincial relations as in most other areas of life, means and ends cannot be separated. Bad form on the golf course produces only a slice or a hook, but bad form in federal-provincial negotiations endangers the unity of our country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
More than any other aspect, it is the form of federal-provincial relations that must change, and it cannot change so long as there exists an insensitive and remote federal government that does not respect the needs and wishes of the provinces. I am not a champion of the provinces against the federal government. The provinces must appreciate and respect the essential roles and powers of the federal government. But they would demonstrate that respect more readily if it were reciprocated or, even better, initiated by the federal government.
I would like to quote from the Conservative party's Kingston communique, which was a joint statement made by our leader and the then four Progressive Conservative premiers after their meeting last September in Kingston. In that document the Conservative party's view of the process of federal-provincial relations was clearly set out. It said:
The federal government must be strong enough financially to influence the economy, bring about equalization of opportunity and stimulate under-developed sectors of the economy. But those national objectives can be attained without the federal government arbitrarily using its spending power, as it has so often in recent years, to force its way into areas of provincial responsibility. We are agreed that the federal spending power must be brought within constitutional bounds so that it never again is used by Ottawa to force action in areas not granted to Ottawa by the constitution.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the attitude of this government is one of take it or leave it. It is one of fiscal manipulation. If you take it you must do such and such. This attitude will not beget a sense of partnership, no matter how much money or how good the
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
idea. Federal-provincial co-operation must be a two-way street; there must be input from the provinces, not just output from Ottawa.
Regional diversity is a fact of life in this country. Economically, politically and socially, the regions have different attitudes, different needs, different aspirations. It is essential that these attitudes, needs and aspirations find expression in federal decision-making. This budget was an opportunity for making that kind of accommodation for regional diversity in national policy. It should have demonstrated that such accommodation is possible. Instead, the episode has aggravated old tensions, reinforced old fears and put up hurdles which it will be difficult to clear if such a measure is attempted again.
The concept of a budget founded on federal-provincial cooperation, a concept which held out and still holds out so much promise, has been made into a travesty by what has gone on in the past several days. That travesty could have been avoided if only the Prime Minister had taken the premiers into his confidence by broaching this concept at the economic summit in February. He chose not to do so. The curtain on this tragedy of errors is now about to fall, but the consequences for the federal system have yet to make their presence felt on the stage. The Minister of Finance cannot escape the authorship of this budget; he and the Prime Minister must also accept the responsibility for the damage that has needlessly resulted from it.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened to and read some of the speeches made on the budget on both sides of the House. Coming as I do from an area that is diversified and probably has a little bit of all Canada, the constituency of Essex-Windsor which I represent-one of the most southerly parts of Canada and a very productive part-I sometimes wonder if I am in dreamland or if I live in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are on cloud nine.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have had the opportunity to represent this country as a member of parliament and as Minister of Agriculture at world meetings, and I can say there is no other country in the world that is envied as is Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are envied for the freedom that we take for granted and for the things in which Canada has given world leadership. We are a northern hemisphere country, a country that many people refer to as the land of ice and snow. I am a representative of my constituency first and foremost. I know, Mr. Speaker, that I could not be Minister of Agriculture in our democratic society in Canada if I had not been elected in my own constituency of Essex-Windsor. Having had the opportunity to represent the people of Canada at many world meetings as Minister of Agriculture, it is hard for me to accept the tremendous admiration that people express for Canada without realizing what Canada is all about.

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
I wonder if some people in this country know what Canada is all about or why Canada even exists today. They should go back in history and find out why this country was created, why we created this confederation called Canada and how it came about. It is one of the most fragile confederations in the whole world, created mainly by two founding nations, the French and the English. Had it not been for those two groups working together, then-and some people may scoff at this-I would probably be the secretary of agriculture for North America! But those two founding nations together said they wanted to be different, that they wanted to be a country called Canada.
When 1 attend these world meetings I am proud that Canada has given leadership in food aid long before it became a "sexy" thing to be involved in and before other countries entered this sphere. My Department of Agriculture was in the forefront of providing help to developing countries and to the poor and underprivileged of this world. Other departments became more involved as time went on because food aid became a "sexy" thing to be involved in.
We have gained a respect that no other nation in the world has, whether it be the United States or the U.S.S.R. Of the 132 nations that attend the World Food Conference meetings, none has the respect that Canada commands. We aid our fellowman no matter where he may be in the world. We help on the basis of need, not because of their political philosophy or whether they are going to join our military alliance or whatever. That is why we are the envy of the world and the jewel of the world.
Sometimes when I sit here listening to dull speeches from the opposition about what a terrible country Canada has turned out to be I cannot believe I am in one of the most democratic parliaments in the world, the Canadian parliament. I can hardly believe I am the peasant child who grew up in Essex county, who was elected to one of the highest positions in the land and then appointed Minister of Agriculture. This is a country that offers a tremendous opportunity to anyone who wants to take it.
I listen to the opposition speak of gloom and doom in this great country that offers more opportunity than any other nation in the world at the present time, knowing that no other nation offers as much. There have been more inquiries from foreign corporations about investment in this country this year than ever before in our history. Does that say that this country is so bad? No, it does not say it is so bad. It says it offers more opportunity for investment than any other country.
We hear talk about the dollar. I see members here who are knowledgeable about agriculture but who say nothing about what the dollar has meant to them. I see people associated with the cattle industry, but they have not said that the dollar has brought the boom days back again to the cattle industry. We do not have an influx of cattle from the United States because our dollar is higher than theirs and they are not shipping cattle to us.
We are paying our debts in Canadian dollars to our banks, to our mortgage holders, to our trust companies and so on, and this has been beneficial to us. Whether it be in world trade,
[Mr. Whelan.)
with cereal grains, oil seeds or whatever you like, this is one of the most beneficial things that has ever happened to us.
Today I heard a member of the opposition criticize the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) for something he said about the dollar's value. If the opposition were honest, they would admit that this has been one of the most beneficial things that has happened, because we have been able to compete in the export of agricultural and industrial products.
We hear talk of gloom and doom in regard to development in our country. Mr. Speaker, when I was elected to this House in 1962 unemployment in my area-the great agricultural, productive area of Essex county within which is the great industrial city of Windsor-stood at 22 per cent. I was raised on a farm but I worked in factories. I know what life in an auto factory or a chemical plant is like because I worked in different occupations. I hear talk today about this great economic depression in this country. I wonder how honest some politicians are when they compare today to the dirty thirties and say this is the greatest economic depression we have seen. I was not in the work force in the 1930's but my older brothers were. I can remember those days and so can others. People were lucky if they worked for board in those days. They dared not take sick as there was no hospitalization, no medicare, no social services.
Let me talk about what is going on in my humble constituency of Essex-Windsor and the area where I live. Last year we had never before issued so many building permits, not only in volume but also in dollar value. In my area at the present time expansion is going on in the industrial sectors. In the agricultural business, which is still very important in that area, the Maple Leaf company is expanding by building a tremendous vegetable oil processing complex which will cost in excess of $50 million. The United Co-operative Company is building a large agricultural complex with an elevator system which will be the most efficient elevator system in Canada and will cost in excess of $22 million. The Redpath company and Labatt's brewery are going into a corn sweetener plant costing approximately $75 million, or maybe $100 million by the time it is finished. All of these things, plus many others, have taken place in that great economically depressed area of southwestern Ontario.
It does me good to go outside Canada and listen to what people say about this country. When I come back I realize how lucky we are to live in this country. All I can say is: "Thank God that we live in Canada".
To come back to my constituency, General Motors Corporation is expanding production facilities which will include 1,500 new jobs by 1980. Chrysler Corporation will be expanding their facilities and increasing manpower in that area. Do these people who will invest millions and billions of dollars in the auto industry in Canada and the United States of America not have confidence in what will take place in the economic makeup of North America? We have those people who print
April 18, 1978

doom and gloom about the auto pact. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is: "Thank God for the auto pact and thank God for those politicians of the past." Some of them are still very active, such as our High Commissioner in Great Britain, the Hon. Paul Martin, who was one of the leaders in the auto pact and who realized the importance of having agreement that a certain portion of the North American auto market belonged to us.
Let us compare that situation to the farm machinery industry where there is no free trade and no such agreement. The hon. member from Winnipeg who is making a lot of noise over there and who will win his election on a hate campaign in Manitoba, should face the fact that maybe there would be a healthier farm machinery industry in western Canada if we did not have the completely free trade program. Maybe it is not so free trade because they are always great defenders when I criticize the U.S. ambassador to Canada as not so liberal in free trade.
Farm machinery parts can be brought into Canada duty free, but a machinery part manufactured in the hon. member's constituency could not be exported to the U.S. duty free, there would be 7 per cent duty. Agricultural chemicals come into Canada duty-free, but going into the United Stales there is about 14 per cent duty. We need more pacts like the auto pact, not less. We can improve upon them as time goes on and as we gain experience. They are not as bad as hon. members try to make them out to be.
The hon. member from Newfoundland pointed out today that my city had some of the most outlandish unemployment figures. He mentioned some figures about St. Catharines and the city of Windsor, but he did not point out the figures from the area where the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) lives. The hon. member for Perth-Wilmot is not in the House tonight; he probably has some other obligations elsewhere and we will excuse him for not being here tonight. But I want to say that there is less than 2 per cent unemployment in the Perth-Wilmot constituency. Maybe that is why he figures it is not necessary for him to participate in the budget debate; he has nothing to worry about in Perth-Wilmot because of the government's actions. That hon. member's constituency has the least unemployment among young people-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why? Because of government policy. The constituency which the hon. member represents probably has some of the highest incomes per farm family in Ontario and the area has possibly the highest farm incomes in Canada. Fifty-four per cent of the constituents have an income of $25,000 plus. This is the result of the healthy agricultural society which we have in Canada.
I am so tired of listening to politicians and even some farm leaders who talk about farm income going down. I received a letter from a so-called farm leader from British Columbia pointing out that farmers' incomes had dropped 9 per cent. Mr. Speaker, do you know how much farm income went up in 1975? At that time it had an increase of 187 per cent.
The Budget-Mr. Whelan

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: From 1971 to 1975 there was an increase of 187 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. Minister of Agriculture has the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
From 1971 to 1975 there was an increase of 187 per cent. Some people talk about it going down 9 per cent and 11 per cent. It has a long way to go down to equal the 187 per cent it went up. Figures are being used out of context. In British Columbia last year net income did not increase the way we would all like to see it, but it was not down, it was up. It increased three points on net income in British Columbia. I can go on and point out other farm production entities in Canada which have looked after themselves and are not doing all that badly. Some members on the other side of the House do not like to admit it.
The Canadian Horticultural Society gave an award this year to a person who had done more than anyone before in the history of the Canadian Horticultural Society.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who received that award?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That award was to the Minister of Agriculture.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If all these people from the Canadian Horticultural Society were Liberals, I could understand that, but I do not think the majority of them are Liberals in that organization. They are honest enough to recognize what this government has done for their organization.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is not one member of the horticultural industry producing those crops who has not benefitted from the action of this government. There is not one that is an efficient producer that does not have a net income that I know of. In addition, we have used stablization programs more since this government has been in power and since I have been Minister of Agriculture than ever before to assist those people in time of need, when they have experienced depressed markets.
I am so tired of hearing talk about farmers who have lost their net income. I wonder how many are honest enough to admit why farm land is higher in value in Canada than it is in the United States. The answer should be plain and simple to them. It is because farm income is generally better in Canada and because farmers, if they are efficient producers, are provided more security in this country than they are in any other nation in the world. None of our programs provide any kind of income for an inefficient producer who is lazy and does not want to work. He or she must work or they will not get

April 18, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Whelan
that kind of living or that kind of net income I have just talked about.
I have heard a lot of members talk about the dairy industry. A number of members who are listening to me tonight were in the House when I presented the new dairy program for 1978-79, but they did not even listen to what I was saying. I am sure a great many of them have not even read the informative briefs we gave them at the time. But I say there is no other country in the whole nation called the world-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, whether we want to recognize it or not, we are citizens of the world, or of a nation called the world. The hon. member is laughing. It is too bad he does not widen his horizons a little because we are citizens of the world whether you want to call it a nation or a lithosphere. We are citizens of that great globe. Some of the members opposite, by their attitude, probably do not want to recognize it is round.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Back to the budget debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone says "back to the budget debate". I do not know what the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) said in the budget debate. I did not read his speech in the media anywhere. If he said anything at all it was probably about some kind of information scheme he was dreaming up which would put money in other people's pockets. He is talking about things in a democracy which have about as much to do with security of a family income as a snowball in hell. I have not received many letters from him lately about anything in his constituency, though in that constituency up in Peace River country even Peter's heritage fund could do a bit more by way of looking after the people there. The province of Alberta has so many billions to spare that they are piling them up. The hon. member for Peace River talks a great deal about Canadianism. If he can say that this heritage fund has created fairness in Canada I should like him some day to explain it to me as a peasant so that I can understand it.
The budget has done much more than most people realize to assist the farm community. Take the part in the budget having to do with research. It means that the private sector engaged in agricultural research can write off 50 per cent of the cost. That is what we want. We want more involvement in agricultural research in the private sector. This is the opportunity for those who have been saying they want to do more in the private sector. They have been given the chance.
I can see the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) agreeing with me even before I make this statement because I know he has the welfare of the average Canadian corporate farm at heart. I do not know whether the hon. member's farm is a corporate farm, but if it is he will now be able to pass it on to his son or daughter free of tax.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was one of my ideas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and I give credit to the hon. member for Medicine Hat, along with a lot of members on this side who made the same kind of recommendation as he did. We wanted to keep all those experienced people in agriculture and not oblige them to buy their farm twice. I want to tell the hon. member something. In many ways he is a great defender of the country to the south of us, though not all the time. Let me ask him whether farmers can do that in the United States of America. He knows they cannot do that in the United States. Even when a former minister of finance permitted the transfer of family farms without taxation to sons or daughters, Mr. Butt, the secretary of agriculture for the United States, said: "You must be out of your cotton-picking minds; we would never do that in the United States".
We have problems in Canadian agriculture but they are not of the magnitude of those experienced in the United States. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has shown his sincerity by listening to the wishes of members of this democratic institution called the House of Commons. He has shown his sincerity by reacting in a receptive way to the demands which have been made for this kind of provision. I know of no other country which would allow this to take place.
Canada, we must remember, was built by farmers. It was built by people who had not been given the opportunity to own land in their country of origin, whether it was the United Kingdom, Scotland, Ireland, France or another of the European countries. Their chance of owning land and building up new democratic institutions was pretty well nil, maybe even minus nil as far as that goes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I recently saw figures for Scotland which showed there are less than a thousand landowners in Scotland, most of them share croppers. That is why agricultural production in Canada is held in such tremendous admiration around the world. Such northern hemisphere countries as Russia, China and so on cannot understand how we are so productive, not only cereals but in dairy products, livestock, poultry and so on. No country is as efficient as we have become. And there is no nation in the world which lets its farmers run its business as we do.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was talking about federal-provincial co-operation. I challenge anyone to look at any federal state and tell me where there is more co-operation between the various departments of agriculture in the field of food production than there is here in Canada. On the other hand, there is no other minister of agriculture in the world who has to deal as I do with such powerful provinces which are concerned with agricultural production.
Do hon. members think the secretary of agriculture of the United States has to call up 52 directors of agriculture in that country before he can make a decision? Not on your bottom dollar. They have authority federally. But we on this side believe in federal-provincial co-operation. We even have a separatist government in Quebec signing agreements with us
April 18, 1978

on such matters as national broiler marketing boards. They recognize this is good for agriculture. They recognize the constitution as it is, because it says agriculture should, first and foremost, be a federal responsibility. It is, and we are fulfilling that responsibility. This is why we are so productive. There is no other group in society which has increased productivity by 300 per cent in the last 25 years. Agriculture has done it. The farmers have accepted every form of automation and scientific break-through. But the incentive to create was there and was provided by government for the last 25 years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The income of those farmers is going down.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have dealt with the hon. member's constituency. He even told me himself he had one of the richest, with one of the lowest rates of unemployment. As humble as the hon. member is, he certainly would not want to take credit for that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope you don't either.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The budget debate could go on for several days, in which case the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot would have an opportunity to take part in it. I am sure he would want to, and if he wants to put the facts on the record, he will tell us how wonderfully the farmers in Perth county are doing. He will tell us all about those things.
I want to say a couple of things about the Minister of Finance. I met Jean Chretien when he first came to Ottawa.

speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I meant the Minister of Finance. I cannot get used to the formality of not being able to call a person by his first name in parliament, because in our rural communities we always do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have been to the Mother of Parliaments. Sometimes I think our parliament has detoured away from the instinct of democratic parliament. I do not want this to be a lesson to you, Mr. Speaker, but recently I visited the House of Commons in the United Kingdom. The members there put their feet up on the Speaker's table. They laid on the benches and nearly went to sleep. I said to one minister afterwards, "Mr. Minister, if we did that in the parliament of Canada, which is on television, we would be run out of the place". That minister brought me down to the ground pretty quickly. He said to me, "Mr. Minister, this is the house of commoners, and it must always have the image of a place for commoners". I sometimes think we detour away from that here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has once again demonstrated to
The Budget-Mr. Whiteway
the country his ability to speak without notes and without facts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He takes pride in the fact that he is born of a humble background. I was born the son of a cobbler from Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The son of a what?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The son of a cobbler from Nova Scotia. Down there the fishermen have a little adage about which the Minister of Agriculture might be aware: Even fish would not find themselves on the hook if they kept their mouths shut.
We are going to be quoting the minister's speech tonight to every farmer in this country, because there will not be a farmer who will not want to hear about the prosperity he has missed for years. We will quote the minister's every word to every farmer, and we will see how the minister's words stand up when and if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dares to issue the writ.
Hon. members opposite speak firmly and boldly, yet it is April 18 and there is no writ of election. Where is the Prime Minister tonight? I expect that he will walk down that aisle opposite with a writ in hand, and when he does, we will see about this decade of progress about which the Minister of Agriculture talks, the Trudeau decade. The Minister of Agriculture is shaking his head. Well, let him go behind the curtain, have a caucus with his leader and see if he has the guts to issue the writ tonight.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but it being 9.45 p.m. it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 60(7), to interrupt the proceedings and put forthwith the amendment now before the House.
The question is on the amendment in the name of the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said amendment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All those opposed will please say nay.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays have it.

The Budget-Mr. Whiteway
